#4476. Toyota Confirms New GR Celica By Announcing 2027 World Rally Championship Car

The heralded sports car nameplate will finally return as part of Toyota’s racing outfit—and then, presumably, on a production car too.

On Tuesday, Toyota officially confirmed that the Celica will return to the Japanese automaker’s family, but its first appearance seemingly won’t be as a production car. Instead, Toyota’s motorsport outfits—Toyota Racing and Gazoo Racing Toyota—will enter two models in the 2027 World Rally Championship ... and one will be a Toyota GR Celica.

The Celica's return has been rumored for years, but this is the first time Toyota has used the official name. Late last year, Cooper Ericksen, Toyota North America’s senior vice president of product planning and strategy, said a model that could be the Celica was in “pretty advanced development.” Now, Toyota says it will have a Celica WRC car ready by late January, when the Rally Monte Carlo will kick off the season.

Welsh rally driver and 2026 WRC title winner Elfyn Evans will head up Toyota Racing’s WRC effort alongside former Gazoo Racing driver Oliver Solberg. Solberg was the runner-up in the 2026 WRC season, narrowly missing the crown after a crash on the final power stage at the Rally Italia Sardegna. Finnish WRC driver Sami Pajari will also join the team.

“Before now, there was a specific regulation that said that for Rally1 homologation, there’s only one model allowed per manufacturer. That regulation has been changed to say, as long as the main mechanical components remain identical, you can do a variant model of your Rally1,” Tom Fowler, technical director of Toyota Gazoo Racing, said to DirtFish. “We had this opportunity to use this as a marketing tool and as a tool to increase the participation and to make things more interesting. There’s not really a big change; in the past we have run four, five or six cars on an event—but they’ve all been the same. This time, instead of running identical cars, we’re going to run two cars.”

Mechanically, this means the current GR Yaris Rally1 and the incoming GR Celica Rally1 will be largely similar. 2027 WRC Rally1 cars will continue to use a spaceframe chassis with turbocharged 1.6-liter inline-four engines and homologated suspension, running gear, and brakes from the current Rally2 category.

Toyota has yet to provide any other details about the Celica rally car beyond its name, but homologation regulations for the 2027 WRC season require production of at least 10 units within 24 months of the homologation date. Additionally, Toyota must be capable of supplying at least 10 race-ready WRC27-type cars per calendar year to customers.

Both of those regulations pertain to rally-specific models, not road-going models. Hence, the announcement that a Celica is coming to WRC doesn’t necessarily confirm the imminent arrival of a road car. Toyota executives previously confirmed the Celica would likely have an internal combustion engine, but declined to provide specific details, and the Celica’s shape, power figures, drivetrain layout, and number of seats have yet to be announced.

The Celica has a long history in WRC, first competing in 1972. Toyota entered the Celica in WRC through the 1980s and 1990s, with Carlos Sainz Sr. taking the drivers' titles in 1990 and 1992. Juha Kankkunen and Didier Auriol continued the Celica winning streak in 1993 and 1994. Toyota’s factory-supported Celica WRC run ended after the automaker earned a year-long WRC ban in 1995 over an illegal turbo restrictor, though privateers continued racing the model later in the 1990s.

#4475. The Car That Fell to Earth: We Test the 1979 Datsun 310-GX

This little Datsun is still getting in touch with reality.

From the May 1979 issue of Car and Driver.

Datsun is not giving up its small-car territory without a fight. All the adver­tising miles on the new 310 are proof of that. For months now, you’ve seen Dat­sun’s new small car zipping across your TV screen, splashed lavishly over maga­zine pages, and blown up bigger than life on roadside billboards. If Datsun is driven to do anything, it’s to sell 310s.

This ad blitz is understandable, be­cause the 310 is Datsun’s new-genera­tion front-wheel-drive car, a key weapon it will use to defend itself in the world­wide small-car war that’s escalating vi­ciously even now. Moreover, it repre­sents Datsun’s second attempt at build­ing a front-drive sedan, since it’s the successor to the ill-fated F-10. As an ac­knowledged small-car giant, Datsun has a reputation to protect.

To these ends, Datsun has armed itself with a pair of all-new three-door se­dans. They’re named simply the 310 se­dan and the 310-GX—which is the sub­ject of this test. A four-door sedan may be sent over later, but for now, just these two constitute the 310 arsenal. The sedan is the family hauler, while the GX is intended to add a dose of sport to the basic 310 theme. For all practical purposes, the two cars are mechanically identical.

See all results for used cars for sale near 07104

The 310 shares its basic layout with the original F-10. It once again has a 1397 cc four-cylinder engine mounted transversely in the chassis and driving the front wheels. Each corner of the unit body is again suspended independently, with MacPherson struts, coil springs, and an anti-sway bar up front, and trail­ing arms and coil springs in the rear. But aside from these superficial similarities to the old F-10, the new 310 is, as they say, new from bumper to bumper.

Which is just fine by us, because the old F-10 just wasn’t suited to life here on spaceship earth. It was, you’ll re­member, an unearthly amalgam of fun­ny shapes and openings, a cramped and noisy little car that always acted a bit tipsy. In fact, given the way the packaging advantages of front-wheel drive were ignored in the F-10, it could well have been designed three thousand miles in outer space instead of that same distance across the Pacific. About the only things you could say in its favor were that its engine, proven in the B-210, was reliable and that it was good in the snow. Not exactly a rave review.

Datsun wants us to forget the past. It's made every attempt to mold the 310 into a car completely different from its predecessor. And if appearances are anything to go by, it’s accomplished that goal. The old banana-with-windows styling has given way to a fresh-cut wedge profile. And while Datsun hasn’t made the 310 any lower, it has made it longer and noticeably wider. For the record, it’s five inches longer and four inches wider, but—at 2600 pounds­—only 80 pounds heavier. Inside, the handsome velour seats, thick carpeting, and color-keyed dash bespeak a new­found awareness of American tastes. And, standard procedure for Japanese carmakers, Datsun has loaded the 310 chock-full of features designed to make life behind the wheel more pleasant.

See all results for used cars for sale near 07104

Every 310, GX or sedan, comes with reclining seats, a split-back folding rear seat, a slider mechanism that moves the passenger’s bucket forward to facilitate rear-seat entry, a quartz clock, a remote hatch opener, side-window defroster vents, intermittent wipers, power brakes, a remote fuel-filler-door open­er, a rear defogger, and a day-night mir­ror. The sedan also features console-­mounted remote cable controls for the flip-out rear windows. The GX adds roll-down rear quarter-windows, a rear window wiper-washer, a tach, a five­-speed transmission, a four-spoke steer­ing wheel, and fatter, 165/70-13 tires. It certainly seems as though Datsun has wedged the 310 right into the heart of small-car country. Yet despite such favorable first impressions, we found—af­ter living with a GX for more than 2000 miles—that all is still not well with Dat­sun’s front-drive car.

The small-car facts of life have been readily defined for Datsun by such front-line front-drivers as the Rabbit, the Strada, the Omni/Horizon, the Fies­ta, the Civic, and now GM’s formidable new X-body compacts. But when you compare it with its competition, the 310 comes off as little more than an F-10 that fell to earth and isn’t quite in touch with reality yet.

The 310’s interior is a perfect exam­ple of the confusing inconsistencies that compromise the car throughout. Datsun obviously went to a lot of trouble to make the 310’s cabin more hospitable than the F-10’s, yet the effect of the handsome carpeting, dash, and uphol­stery is offset by door panels that look plain enough to have come out of a Dat­sun pickup. Datsun also widened the car to achieve more interior width. This al­leviates the phone-booth claustropho­bia of the F-10—but only for front-seat passengers; rear-seat riders are almost as cramped as they were in the older car. In both new cars, rear legroom is still in severely short supply. Other front-drive cars with the same wheel­base do much better in this respect.

Where the GX really falls down on the job is in the all-important area of day-to-day livability. The 310 is so rid­dled with annoying quirks that its posi­tive qualities are overshadowed.

Take the radio, for instance. Please. Our test car had the optional AM/FM unit. Besides impoverished reception, it was endowed with what has to be one of this decade’s worst speakers—mounted under the dash, facing the floor. Most of the music we could tune in became bad­ly garbled when the volume was turned up loud enough to be heard during highway cruising. You don’t have to lis­ten to the radio, of course, but you’ll find the heating system harder to avoid. When you do use it, you’ll find it only marginally effective. Worse yet, the de­froster—which has to work overtime to get the job done—is about as quiet as an idling 747.

And if you want a little whine before dinner, the 310’s trans­mission will be more than happy to oblige—in any gear. Though the 310’s shift linkage is much improved over the F-10’s Silly Putty unit, the transmission crunched almost every time we grabbed third gear. Then there’s the matter of the shift pattern, which has first down and to the left, off of the H, and re­verse—with no protective lockout­—dead ahead, where any self-respecting low gear ought to be. And sure enough, there is the occasional gnashing of re­verse when making the one-two shift.

Then again, we didn’t like reverse much anyway, because selecting it brought on the annoying warning beeper that is Datsun’s fix for the shift-pattern prob­lem. (It’s there to prevent the unwary from backing away from stoplights when they put the shifter where first is in most other cars.) Last but not least was the vibration problem. At idle, the GX’s engine was so rough that the steering wheel actually got a little blurry around the edges. Nudging the idle up about 100 rpm would solve that prob­lem, but only the engineers will be able to quiet the sharp buzzing of the ex­haust system as the revs climb past 5000—a sound that is the essence of tin­niness. Most of these problems also cropped up on a 310 sedan we were sampling, so they seem to be basic de­sign flaws, not isolated failings of the GX test car.

All of this, when added to the below­ average space utilization, makes the 310 rough-edged—even crude—given the current level of small-car sophistication. That’s unfortunate, because it’s due cause for avoiding what is essentially a fun car to drive. The little engine revs up willingly, and the five-speed—top gear is a direct 1:1 ratio—helps you make good use of the available power. The steering response is direct, and there’s plenty of road feel. Once you get used to the suspension’s initial rubberi­ness when you first twist the wheel, the GX turns out to be a fine fling-around car. It’s also quite stable during highway cruising, and it rides acceptably as well. And of course it’s stingy with your gas money, returning 27 miles for every EPA gallon.

But decent road manners are only part of what makes a good small car. The 310 represents a Datsun move in the right direction, but little more; that it’s superior to the F-10 is frankly not one of the world’s outstanding accom­plishments. This is underscored by the fact that $5500 will probably also buy a well-equipped GM X-body compact. And the 310 can’t begin to match the X­ car’s room, ride, quietness, appoint­ments, and overall refinement—yet its economy is only marginally better. The 310 isn’t in the same league.

So at this point the best news we have is that Datsun’s front-drive car has final­ly come down to earth. But if it’s to live here happily, Datsun will have to try still harder—a lot harder.

Since the subject of this test is the 310 sport coupe, I’ll have to add my vote to the negative side. And that’s too bad, be­cause condemning the sport coupe can, by extension, condemn the sedan that came, afterthought-like, with the deal. My strongest negatives about the sport coupe are its looks (really ugly) and its transmission (really terrible). I don’t have either of those complaints about the sedan. In fact, I think Datsun’s marketeers are in for a surprise. Despite their studied predictions, my hunch is the sporty version will be shunned in the showroom (”Yes, Harry. It’s true. It’s the dreaded Show­room Shun”), and the boxy but cute, sim­ple but contemporary sedan will find favor. And that’s the way it should be, be­cause the 310 sedan is—in the Datsun tradition—a functional, sensible, straightfor­ward transportation module, and that’s what a lot of people are looking for these days. They don’t want an overstyled, beeping aggravation. —Mike Knepper

The Datsun 310, like the Subaru, makes us wonder if there is not a streak of automotive perversity loose among America’s car buyers, and if Datsun may not be on to something big. The 310 simply does not address itself to creature comfort in the way that a Toyota or a Honda does. It is a rather Spartan car, with lots of engine and transmission noise, and very little iso­lation from the mechanical realities. There’s an old-fashioned rough-and­-readiness about the 310 that’s not masked by velour upholstery or cut-pile carpets­—a sort of naïve innocence that appealed to me, along with my belief that it would probably run forever—but I couldn’t ex­plain my affectionate regard for these attributes to my co-testers. Noisy little cars that bucket along as the Datsun does are fun. They bring out an adolescent streak in me that 30 years of automotive experi­ence has been insufficient to suppress. They are amusingly likable in their imper­fections—the four-speed sedan more so than the more pretentious coupe. The 310 didn’t try to kid me, nor did it ever let me down. Only when I learned how much I’d have to pay for those simple, earthy pleasures did my enthusiasm start to flag. —David E. Davis Jr.

#4474. Kia racks up another record month as its new $30K electric SUV hits dealers

Kia is eyeing its fourth consecutive annual US sales record after another record-breaking October. With the new 2027 EV3 arriving, Kia is “confident” the momentum will carry into Q4 and well into 2027.

“With six consecutive months of record-breaking sales, Kia is accelerating toward a fourth straight annual sales record,” Kia America vice president of sales Eric Watson said on Tuesday.

Kia sold 80,008 vehicles in the US last month, up 16% year over year and marking its best October sales month ever.

Kia said electrified and hybrid vehicles drove the growth, with sales up 112% and 114% YOY, both setting new sales records.

Several Kia models posted strong YOY sales growth, including the three-row electric EV9 (+111%), Telluride (+63%), EV6 (+58%), Seltos (+43%), Sorento (+31%), Carnival (+17%), K4 (+14%), and Sportage (+12%).

Regarding its fully electric vehicles. Sales of the EV9, Kia’s three-row electric SUV, are now up 5% year-to-date, with 13,835 units sold through October.

Although EV6 sales rebounded slightly last month, they are still down 39% YTD, with 7,067 units sold through October.

Kia’s new entry-level electric SUV, the EV3 (check out our review), is now in showrooms nationwide. After it went on sale in mid-August, Kia sold 1,496 EV3s in its first two months.

The 2027 EV3 is Kia’s most affordable fully electric vehicle, starting at $29,890. That’s for the base EV3 Light model, which uses a 58.3 kWh battery that provides up to 221 miles of range.

Higher-priced trims, including the Wind, Land, GT-Line, and GT, use an 81.4 kWh battery for up to 321 miles of range.

Front-wheel-drive (FWD) models have a single 201-horsepower electric motor. Upgrading to all-wheel-drive (AWD) costs $3,200 and adds a rear electric motor for a combined 261 horsepower.

All variants have a native NACS port so that drivers can use Tesla Superchargers without a separate adapter. Charging the 58.3 kWh battery from 10% to 80% takes around 29 minutes, while the larger 81.4 kWh battery takes about 31 minutes.

Inside, all EV3 models feature Kia’s latest ccNC (connected car Navigation Cockpit) with standard wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

The setup provides nearly 30″ of combined digital screens, including a dual 12.3″ instrument cluster and touchscreen infotainment, plus a 5″ climate control display.

Kia describes the EV3 as an “entry-level EV SUV that offers many of the advanced amenities of the EV9,” but in a smaller, more affordable package.

The 2027 Kia EV9 starts at $54,990. That’s also for the base EV9 Light short-range trim, which uses a 76.1 kWh battery with up to 230 miles of range.

Higher-priced trims, including the Light Long Range, Wind, Land, and GT-Line, use a larger 99.8 kWh battery that delivers up to 305 miles of range in RWD variants.

Kia’s three-row electric SUV offers up to 42.8″ of legroom in the second row, which is even more than the 2025 Cadillac Escalade. Buyers can choose from six- and seven-seat configurations.

“An expanding hybrid lineup, the arrival of the all-new, all-electric EV3, and the success of the all-new Telluride and Seltos are adding even more momentum to our growth,” Watson said. #4473. Tesla Warned Owners Not To Test Emergency Drive Away. Some Did Anyway.

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Tesla recently rolled out a new feature that will allow owners to drive away from a Supercharger in an emergency. That feature came with an asterisk that Tesla was abundantly clear about: Don't hit it unless you absolutely need to, or else.

Well, a few owners were curious about what would happen if they decided not to heed that warning and activate the feature while plugged into a Tesla Supercharger. And now, through the magic of social media, we now know exactly what happens when an owner flips the switch.

But first, let's talk about what we know happens when a user tries to activate Emergency Drive Away. The driver first gets a warning that requires them to acknowledge the potential for damage to both their car and the Supercharger. If they choose to hit the Activate button and proceed, the Supercharger will unlock from the charge port so the owner can hit the gas and let the charging handle break away.

Again, this is for an emergency where users need to get away, and get away fast. The cost of damage to the car and the Supercharger are probably worth the owner's safety. That's why Tesla requires that any vehicle which activates Emergency Drive Away visit a Service Center so that the car can be assessed for damage before the warning can be cleared.

One owner who decided to ignore this warning was reportedly hit with a $539 fee for Tesla's service department to inspect their car's charge port. That's despite not actually driving an inch.

Another user on Reddit reported that they wanted to test what would happen "out of curiosity." They tested it in the same way—immediately putting the car in park and not driving an inch before manually pulling the charger out of the car to avoid damaging any of the equipment.

To their surprise, the car displayed an error that could not be cleared except by Tesla service and the Supercharger was pulled out of service. Fortunately, Tesla's service marked their service inspection as "goodwill" and did not charge the driver.

Another owner reported an initial estimate of $255 but ultimately left their service appointment with a $33.15 bill. A different owner was invoiced $178.20 for an inspection following their own curiosity.

Not all tests—whether intentional or not—have been without damage. Another owner on Reddit witnessed a vehicle activate the feature at a public charger and drive away.

The charger stall can be seen flexing from the cable yank and a component hit the ground behind the car, which means that driver may not be as fortunate to receive a no-cost visit to the Service Center as some of the other beta testers have experienced.

The potential bill gets even uglier if Tesla decides to begin charging for potential Supercharger repairs. Costs to the car aside, Tesla says repairing a Supercharger stall damaged by Emergency Drive Away "can be up to $25k."

There is probably room to make activation of this feature harder. But then again, Tesla may not want to make it harder to get away in an emergency. A financial penalty and mandatory post-activation service visit should (in theory) be enough to dissuade owners from activating it when they don't need to. But as we've seen from the above, that might not be the case.

#4472. The Range Rover Evoque and Velar Won’t Live Past 2027

But don’t worry if you’re not in the upper 1%; JLR has plans to keep affordable Land Rover models in the mix.

Update, 11/3 1:30pm: Jaguar Land Rover has confirmed to Road & Track that the Velar and Evoque will be discontinued: "Both Range Rover Velar and Range Rover Evoque will continue to be sold in selected global markets where demand remains strong, throughout 2027. Production of both models will end in mid-2027 in line with their natural product lifecycles, as JLR's manufacturing facilities transition to build its next generation of vehicles. Solihull will continue to focus on producing Range Rover, Range Rover Sport and the forthcoming Jaguar Type 01, while Halewood will transition to produce the new Range Rover GT and a new model from the Defender family."

The Range Rover Velar and Evoque could soon be facing the axe, as a new report from Autocar contends that both of Range Rover’s smaller, entry-level models won’t see a new generation.

The report cites Martin Limpert, Range Rover’s global managing director, as saying both the Evoque and Velar will be produced through 2027, but not beyond. The current generation Evoque was revealed all the way back in 2018 and went through a mid-cycle refresh for the 2024 model year. Meanwhile, the Velar is even older, having been revealed in 2017. It too was treated to a mid-cycle refresh for 2024.

The elimination of both the Evoque and Velar would significantly increase the cost barrier to entry for a car with the Range Rover badge on it. It would also leave the “Range Rover” brand with only a few models—those being the traditional Range Rover, Range Rover Sport, and incoming Range Rover GT.

But that might not be such a terrible thing. Instead of targeting the lower end of the market with Range Rover-branded models, JLR appears ready to use both its Defender and Discovery brands for those endeavors. Reports of a smaller Defender model suggest it could easily take the place of the Evoque, and JLR has confirmed a new model of some sort will be joining the Defender line. Meanwhile, the Discovery already comes in around the same price as a Velar.

Both the Evoque and Velar launched as relatively controversial projects, but ultimately led to JLR increasing sales numbers. Applying the Range Rover badge to smaller and more affordable cars was a way to make the brand more accessible, and plenty of folks were happy to jump on the train. It even opened some strange doors, with the Range Rover Evoque Convertible being the weirdest of them all. When the Evoque and Velar finally exit, they’ll join the Discovery Sport that’s confirmed to end production this year.

#4471. Chevy Reportedly Axes Plans for the Corvette SUV and EV

It seems like the Corvette will remain a line of V-8 sports cars, as the rumored expansion of the brand to include other models is no longer in the cards.

The imagined future of a broad lineup of Corvette-badged SUVs, sedans, and electric vehicles that some of us dreamed about—or perhaps dreaded—is no longer set to become a reality. GM’s long-rumored plans to build out the Corvette brand as a broader lineup have been shelved, according to a report by GM Authority citing sources within the company.

We’ve been discussing the possibility of a Corvette SUV for years now, and this Porsche Cayenne–fighting model appears to be the most significant casualty of this news. Electric power had also been discussed for a future Corvette, and Chevrolet does currently offer two hybrid powertrains in the C8 Corvette, but it now sounds like GM’s upcoming electric-vehicle platforms won’t be making their way into any models with a Corvette badge. The report even mentions rumors of a four-door Corvette sedan that now isn’t likely to ever see the light of day.

See all results for new 2027 Chevrolet Corvette Stingray / Grand Sport for sale near 60614

This potential Corvette spin-off series could have been a cash cow for GM, much like how the large sales volumes and profits of Porsche’s SUV models help fund its sports-car development. But perhaps GM’s decision hinges on the softer demand for EVs lately, or the backlash it anticipated from Corvette loyalists who might think that offering a Corvette-badged SUV sullies the iconic name. Because GM had never officially announced these plans to begin with, it’s all a bit murky, and Chevrolet representatives said they had nothing to add to this speculation when Car and Driver reached out for comment.

Plus, even without these additional body styles and powertrain choices, it’s not as if the existing Corvette lineup lacks variety. The current C8-generation car offers a wide range of models from the base Stingray and Grand Sport all the way up to the hardcore Z06 and mega-powerful ZR1 variants. Chevy is also surely hard at work on the C9-generation Corvette, as it has already previewed future Corvette models with a recent concept car called the California Corvette.

#4470. This electric microcar just got a 50 mph upgrade, plus a secret Turbo mode

The adorable little Eli ZERO electric microcar is growing up. At this year’s EICMA motorcycle show in Milan, Eli Electric Vehicles is unveiling a faster, more powerful version of its pint-sized electric car, along with a sporty new limited-edition model that even includes a hidden Turbo mode.

First teased last week, the new Eli ZERO MX is the company’s first L7e-class electric vehicle, allowing it to reach speeds of up to 80 km/h (50 mph). That’s a significant jump from the 45 km/h (28 mph) top speed of the original L6e version that we originally reviewed, opening the door to a much wider range of driving scenarios.

And perhaps most importantly, the company managed to squeeze that extra performance into the same tiny package.

The Eli ZERO MX retains the original’s ultra-compact 2.25-meter (7.4-foot) length, making it considerably smaller than even the smallest conventional passenger cars.

But under that tiny exterior, the MX now packs up to 20 kW (27 hp) of peak power, compared to the 12 kW (16 hp) of the original Eli ZERO.

The upgraded model also features a 14.4 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery, providing a claimed range of up to 200 km (124 miles) per charge.

That’s a pretty respectable figure for a vehicle designed primarily for short urban and suburban trips.

The rear-wheel-drive microcar features selectable ECO and SPORT driving modes, a 30% climbing capability, and a tight 7.2-meter turning circle. Charging is handled by a 3.3 kW onboard charger, allowing owners to plug in at home or use public AC charging stations.

Despite its diminutive size, the Eli ZERO MX also includes a surprisingly long list of features normally associated with much larger cars.

Those include air conditioning and heating, a panoramic moonroof, soft-close doors, keyless entry and start, electric power steering, ABS, front and rear disc brakes, and an electronic parking brake.

There’s also an 8.8-inch digital instrument cluster, a reversing camera with rear radar, and an optional 10.1-inch infotainment display with Apple CarPlay.

The MX is available in four colors: Pearl White, Arctic Silver, Graphite, and Champagne.

The biggest difference, though, is the vehicle’s classification. While the original Eli ZERO falls under Europe’s L6e light quadricycle category, the new MX qualifies as an L7e heavy quadricycle. That means it generally requires a higher-level driving license, but also allows for considerably more performance.

For drivers who love the idea of a tiny electric runabout but need something capable of keeping up with faster suburban traffic, the MX could be a much more compelling option.

Eli isn’t stopping at a faster version of its microcar.

The company is also introducing the Eli ZERO Race Edition, a limited-production model available in both the original L6e and the new L7e configurations.

Finished in an exclusive Turbo Red paint job, the Race Edition features racing stripes across the hood, roof, and body panels, along with a rear spoiler and special wheel badging.

Inside, the sporty treatment continues with a two-tone Race Red microsuede and light gray interior, including special upholstery, dashboard accents, and embroidered seats.

But the most interesting feature isn’t immediately visible.

Eli has included a secret Turbo mode activated by pressing and holding the hazard light button. After four quick chimes, the digital instrument cluster switches to Turbo mode and the car’s acceleration response becomes sharper.

Importantly, the feature doesn’t increase the vehicle’s top speed or exceed its regulatory performance limits. Instead, it changes the way the car responds to accelerator inputs, giving it a sportier driving feel.

It’s a fun little Easter egg in a vehicle that already has plenty of personality.

Eli is also offering a new Carbon Aero Kit, consisting of a carbon fiber front splitter, side skirts, and rear wing. The kit is compatible with both the Race Edition and other Eli ZERO models.

Eli has spent years developing its vision of a smaller, lighter, and more efficient alternative to conventional cars, particularly for the short trips that make up much of our daily driving.

The company has already launched its second-generation Eli ZERO, which shares the same 96V electrical architecture and aluminum chassis as the new MX.

By expanding into the L7e category, Eli is addressing one of the biggest limitations of its original design: speed.

A 28 mph (45 km/h) microcar makes plenty of sense in dense urban centers, but its usefulness quickly drops off when drivers need to venture onto faster roads. A 50 mph (80 km/h) version, on the other hand, could make the same tiny vehicle practical for considerably more people.

In the US, this could go pretty much anywhere that didn't require highway driving. Perfect one-and-a-halfth car.

The Eli ZERO family is currently available through authorized dealers in several European markets, including Italy, Norway, and the Netherlands, with prices starting at €10,500 (approximately US $12,000) for the base model. Pricing for the new MX and Race Edition hasn’t yet been announced.

Eli also has a pilot program underway in the United States, though the new models are being introduced primarily for the European market.

Both the Eli ZERO MX and Race Edition will be on display at EICMA 2026 in Milan from November 3–8.

For a vehicle that takes up less than half the space of a conventional car, the Eli ZERO is certainly finding ways to make a bigger impression!

#4469. Volvo Is Getting Crushed In The U.S.

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Volvo is having some trouble adapting to the fast-paced auto market changes in the U.S. From flip-flopping tariffs to the exodus of its sister brand, Polestar, there have been a ton of changes in a relatively short period of time that has been difficult for the Swedes to keep up with.

In its third-quarter earnings call last week, Volvo's leadership admitted that it was struggling to make its endeavors in the U.S. lucrative and that customer optimism in the brand has hit a point not seen in half a century.

"U.S. has proven to be a difficult market to find profitability," said Volvo's Chief Commercial Officer, Erik Severinson, during the company's third quarter earnings call last week. "The consumer sentiment in the U.S. [...] is at a 50-year low."

CEO Hakan Samuelsson said that one of Volvo's oversights was how tariffs would affect its business in the States. He admitted that the company "should have realized" that the tariffs were a real possibility and that they would need to "localize more in the U.S." to address them. The CEO went on to say that Volvo is working to address those tariff-related shortcomings to help strengthen its position in the market.

One of the long-standing ways that Volvo anticipated reversing its sales slump was with the EX60. However, the electric SUV meant to compete with the likes of the BMW iX3 and Mercedes-Benz GLC Electric has proven to be a manufacturing challenge. And with EV sales continuing to boom in Europe and other global electrification hotspots, Americans hoping to get an EX60 in their driveway will be waiting longer than originally anticipated while Europe is prioritized.

The CEO also rather publicly addressed the U.S. falling behind of EV adoption.

Without criticizing, Samuelsson noted that Volvo needs to ensure that its offerings in America would address this. Its plant in South Carolina—which is only running at 20% capacity building the Volvo EX90 (and soon the XC60)—is planned for a second new, multi-powertrain vehicle by the top of the decade.

"The U.S. is electrifying slower than the rest of the world. We need to have a new car that is also flexible in that respect, with all-electric, plug-in or hybrid," said Samuelsson.

Volvo is in a tough spot. Like many other automakers, it went all-in on electrification at the same time when other global automakers committed to building all-EV brands. But as the American market reversed course, Volvo pulled what would have otherwise been high-volume BEV vehicles (the EX30 and EX40) for the U.S. market.

The Swedes now recognize that they need to regain traction in one of the world's most important auto markets. That will come through localization to avoid tariffs, and a push for demand through multiple powertrains. Will it work? Well, that's to be seen.

#4468. Dodge Confirms Return to the NASCAR Cup Series in 2027

The brand used the 2026 SEMA Show to announce it’s completing its fast-track return to NASCAR with Kaulig Racing.

On Monday night at the 2026 SEMA Show, Dodge announced its long-awaited return to the NASCAR Cup Series after a 14-year absence.

This move has been anticipated since its Stellantis-partnered truck brand, Ram, returned to the Craftsman Truck Series this year. With it, Kaulig Racing—which has been operating its five-truck Ram team, will be the first to move over to Dodge.

Dodge’s return is being fast-tracked, moving into the sport after two generations removed. But to Stellantis North America head of American brands, North America marketing and retail strategy Tim Kuniskis, this approach is the only way. As Dodge looks to recenter “gasoline-powered performance,” as its North Star, the only stage truly suitable is the top level of NASCAR.

“Everyone said it was impossible to get back in one year. We said, 'Watch this,'" said Kuniskis. "Sure, we could spend three years planning, testing and perfecting ... or we could do all three in real time, on the track. It's going to be exponentially harder this way. But slow has never been part of Dodge DNA. LFG."

When Dodge last raced at the Cup Series level, it was the end of the Generation 5 era with a race car wearing the Dodge Charger’s face. The Cup car has changed drastically since then through two generations, running the 7 Gen or ’Next Gen’ car since 2022.

The driver announcement is set for this weekend during NASCAR Championship Weekend at Homestead-Miami. Currently, Kaulig Racing runs Ty Dillon in the number 10 and AJ Allmendinger in the No. 16, and the driver lineup is not expected to change. The only wrench thrown into the mix is the unexpected availability of Brad Keselowski, who left RFK—a team he owns 20 percent of—due to disagreements about his future role with the company and his desire to keep racing as long as possible.

Keselowski and Dodge have a special bond, with Keselowski delivering Dodge and Penske Racing a championship in 2012, their farewell season in the sport. “I would say everything's on the table,” Keselowski said during his press conference at Martinsville last weekend. “I have not had a discussion with Dodge or Ram. I'm certainly very open-minded to it alongside all of the OEMs. I haven't given up on a relationship with Ford in the future as well, along with the other two OEMs of Chevrolet and Toyota. Everything's on the table right now for me.”

Kaulig Racing team owner Matt Kaulig founded the team in 2016, four seasons after Dodge first left the sport in the Xfinity (now O’Reilly) Series and then in 2020 at the Cup level with Chevrolet. “This is a very exciting moment for both Chris Rice and me. We launched Kaulig Racing a decade ago and have overcome so many challenges together, which makes it even more remarkable to be announced as the anchor team for Dodge’s return to the NASCAR Cup Series. What a monumental time to be a member of Kaulig Racing,” he said.

Dodge will have a major presence this year at the Snowball Derby, the premier off-season 300-lap pavement super late model race in Pensacola, Florida, held every December. Their new Next Gen NASCAR Cup Car—presumably Charger-branded and inspired—will be revealed on Friday, December 4th. Later that weekend, the brand will also host the Dodge Sno-Brawl, featuring celebrity drivers racing in Dodge Charger Late Models.

Her daily driver is a 2010 Subaru that she refused to do the smallest amount of preventative maintenance on. #4467. 1985 Ford F-250 Restomod Sends Raptor Brand to the ’80s at SEMA

Matt Johnson’s 1985 F-250 Raptor-inspired build was backed by Ford Performance and will be part of Ford’s display at SEMA this year.

Ford’s first Raptor didn’t arrive until 2008 at the 41st Baja 1000 in Ensenada, Mexico. The high-performance F-150 SVT Raptor-R had a podium finish, and the Raptor name continues to grace the widened bodywork of some of Ford’s most powerful pickups.

But imagine if Raptor had come around about two decades earlier. It might’ve looked like Matt Johnson’s Raptor-inspired 1985 F-250, which is getting a huge reveal at Ford’s SEMA booth this year.

The F-250 project actually started with an old Toyota Land Cruiser, which Johnson had planned to put an EcoBoost engine into. A call to Ford Racing Parts led to discussions about a collaboration between the automaker and Johnson, who restores older off-roading vehicles and documents the process on social media.

See all results for new 2027 Ford Super Duty for sale near 95014

A few months later, Ford suggested putting a small-block Heritage motor in the Land Cruiser. Johnson bounced back with a photo of a 1985 F-250 with a blown engine that had been sitting behind his shop. He felt the small-block was better suited for a classic Ford, and the bullnose F-250 seemed like a perfect candidate.

Soon, Johnson’s $800 shop truck, called Norma Jeane, was getting a full makeover backed by Ford Performance. The truck’s original engine was replaced with Ford Racing’s 575-hp 460-cubic-inch Boss V-8. He paired the small-block with a Ford R680 six-speed automatic transmission.

Johnson documented the transformation through a 92-part series on social media. His daily updates covered everything, from installing a custom-made suspension kit to weatherstripping the windows. Though a lot of the truck is now brand new, the F-250 maintains its distinctly ‘80s qualities, right down to the hubcaps and vintage-style stereo.

The build was originally meant to be completed in 40 days, but when Ford proposed the idea of bringing it to SEMA, that 40-day timeline shifted to a much longer saga. Along the way, Johnson has accumulated 425,000 followers on Instagram and even more on Facebook under his Doc Johnson Restorations shop account. His latest post shows the F-250 getting loaded into a transport truck and beginning the journey from his small shop in Klamath Falls, Oregon, to SEMA in Las Vegas.

“Honestly, it’s a crazy story, and I feel blessed to be a part of it,” Johnson said in a press release. “The truck—and the project itself—took on a life of its own. In many ways, I’m just along for the ride.” Johnson and his Raptor-inspired F-250 will be a part of Ford’s display at SEMA, which takes place November 3-6 in Las Vegas, Nevada.

#4466. Zero Motorcycles unveils $8K electric motorcycle, street-legal dirt bike, and much more

Zero Motorcycles is celebrating its 20th anniversary with a major wave of announcements at EICMA 2026, unveiling several new electric two-wheelers alongside some important technology upgrades that could make its existing motorcycles even more appealing.

The biggest news is an entirely new lightweight electric street motorcycle known as Project Ventura, designed to bridge the gap between the increasingly popular world of electric bikes plus lightweight e-motos and the full-size electric motorcycle market. But that’s far from the only news coming out of Zero’s booth in Milan.

The electric motorcycle maker is also announcing a new street-legal version of its XE electric dirt bike that was previously only street-legal in Europe, introducing its LS3 electric scooter to Europe, introducing a redesigned smartphone app, and sharing more details about its upcoming DC fast-charging system.

There’s quite a bit to unpack here, so let’s get into it.

Perhaps the most exciting announcement is Project Ventura, a new lightweight electric motorcycle that Zero hopes will attract an entirely new generation of riders.

With supermoto-inspired styling, 17-inch wheels, and a more approachable design than the company’s larger street motorcycles, Ventura appears aimed squarely at riders who want something more substantial than a typical lightweight e-moto but aren’t necessarily looking for a full-size, high-performance motorcycle.

And with a targeted price of less than US $8,000, it could be one of Zero’s most accessible street motorcycles yet.

The bike features a new electric powertrain producing over 20 kW (27 hp) of peak power, delivering a sustained top speed of 65 mph (105 km/h) and a momentary maximum speed of 81 mph (130 km/h).

That’s a particularly interesting distinction, as it positions the bike as being able to briefly reach highway-capable speeds with the occasional burst of extra performance, but perhaps not for longer sustained highway stretches.

Importantly, we don’t yet know the battery capacity, though Zero is giving us a hint by publishing a range estimate. The company is quoting an estimated real-world range of 93 miles (150 km), but without a real battery capacity figure to parse, it’s hard to take that range estimate at face value.

We do know that the bike will feature onboard Level 2 charging, allowing riders to plug into public AC charging stations without carrying around a separate external charger – something more common on the smallest of electric motorcycles that attempt to cut down on weight and cost by using an off-board charger.

Other features include standard ABS, Bluetooth connectivity, integration with Zero’s upcoming smartphone app, and a chassis designed to accommodate a passenger.

The riding position is upright, and the bike’s supermoto-inspired geometry is intended to deliver agile handling and a playful riding experience.

Perhaps most interestingly, Zero isn’t hiding the fact that it sees the explosion of e-bikes and smaller electric motos as a potential gateway to motorcycle ownership.

“When we set out to build Project Ventura, we had three guiding principles: first, build a bike so good-looking you’d want its poster above your bed. Second, make it a proper electric motorcycle that feels like a natural next step for the millions of riders who’ve spent the last four or five years on e-bikes and e-motos. And third, make it ridiculously fun to ride,” explained Jim Callahan, Zero’s Chief Product and Partnerships Officer.

That’s a notable strategy for a company that has historically focused heavily on higher-performance electric motorcycles. However, the launch of Zero’s smaller Sur Ron-style electric dirt bikes last summer showed that the motorcycle maker did see the writing on the wall in terms of the success of the e-moto market compared to larger flagship bikes.

Instead of trying to convince existing gasoline motorcycle riders to make the electric switch, Zero is increasingly looking toward younger riders who may have already fallen in love with electric two-wheelers and are ready for something faster and more capable.

But for those interested in the new Ventura, they’ll have to wait just a bit longer. The motorcycle is expected to become available in summer 2027.

Another major announcement is a new street-legal version of Zero’s XE electric dirt bike.

The original XE was introduced as part of Zero’s more affordable X Line of lightweight electric off-road motorcycles, offering a more accessible entry point to the brand than its traditional street and dual-sport models. While the model was available in street-legal format in Europe, the US versions were purely off-road affairs.

Now Zero is taking that same general concept and making it legal for public roads, opening up significantly more riding possibilities.

The new XE is fully homologated and features the necessary street equipment, including a headlight, taillight, and centrally mounted dashboard. A small integrated flyscreen and black bodywork give the motorcycle a more refined appearance, while wide dual-sport tires help it transition between pavement and dirt.

Zero has also revised the gearing, using a rear sprocket designed to balance off-road performance with the higher speeds required for street riding.

The result is a claimed top speed of 60 mph (97 km/h), making the XE capable of considerably more than simply putting around the neighborhood, though with a slight torque sacrifice.

For riders who live near off-road riding areas, the appeal is obvious. Instead of loading a dirt bike into a truck or trailer to reach the trails, owners could potentially ride directly from home to the trailhead, provided local regulations allow it.

That’s a particularly useful capability for a lightweight electric dirt bike, where much of the appeal comes from its simplicity, low maintenance, and ability to explore places that larger motorcycles might struggle to reach.

The new street-legal XE is expected to launch in spring 2027, with pricing starting at US $6,295.

Zero is also expanding its electric scooter offerings with the European debut of the LS3, a faster and more capable scooter designed for urban transportation and longer commutes.

While Zero has traditionally been associated with electric motorcycles, its growing interest in scooters represents another effort to reach riders who prioritize everyday transportation over outright performance.

The LS3 offers a top speed of 75 mph (121 km/h), which puts it well beyond the typical low-speed urban electric scooter category.

Zero also quotes a range of up to 93 miles (150 km), powered by a battery system consisting of three onboard batteries with a combined capacity of 5.6 kWh.

Interestingly, one of those batteries is removable and located beneath the seat. Riders can remove it to free up additional storage space, offering some flexibility between maximum battery capacity and cargo-carrying convenience.

That could prove useful for commuters who don’t always need the scooter’s full range but would appreciate extra room for everyday items.

The LS3 also comes equipped with heated grips and a heated seat, features that should be particularly welcome to European riders commuting through colder months.

Connected technology rounds out the package, including compatibility with Zero’s upcoming smartphone app.

The LS3 is expected to become available in Europe in spring 2027.

Beyond the new vehicles, Zero is also working on a redesigned smartphone application that promises to give riders considerably more control over their motorcycles.

The new app is being developed for the LS3, 2027 Street and Dual Sport motorcycles, and Project Ventura.

One of the more interesting features is the ability to customize riding modes. In addition to preset modes that adjust power delivery and regenerative braking, riders will be able to create a custom mode and individually tune parameters including speed, power, torque, and regeneration.

The app will also include a charging-station finder, allowing riders to search for nearby chargers and filter them by charging speed, network, and availability. Apple Maps integration will provide route guidance to selected charging locations.

An optional ride-history feature can automatically record trips, including their distance, duration, and route previews.

Riders will also be able to customize their motorcycle’s dashboard layout, choosing which information appears in each quadrant of the display.

Battery management is getting some attention, too. The app will provide controls for scheduled charging, target charge levels, charging limits, and long-term battery storage settings.

Zero is also adding integrated feedback and support tools that allow owners to report problems or suggest improvements directly through the app, including photos and diagnostic logs.

The redesigned app is expected to arrive in 2027.

Perhaps the most consequential technology announcement, at least for riders who want to take their electric motorcycles beyond short commutes and weekend rides, is Zero’s continued development of DC fast charging.

Zero says it is targeting a 2027 launch for its new fast-charging system, which will support compatible Street and Dual Sport motorcycles.

The system is being designed to charge compatible batteries from 20% to 80% in less than 30 minutes.

That’s a major improvement in convenience compared to the longer AC charging stops that have traditionally been associated with Zero motorcycles.

Importantly, the company is developing the system for both North America and Europe, with different charging connectors for each market.

European motorcycles will use the CCS standard, while North American models will feature NACS connectors.

The latter is particularly interesting given the growing adoption of NACS charging infrastructure across North America, potentially making it easier for electric motorcycle riders to access a wider range of charging locations.

Zero is also developing a retrofit option for eligible existing motorcycles, meaning some current owners may eventually be able to upgrade their bikes rather than purchasing entirely new models to take advantage of the technology.

The company hasn’t yet announced pricing or a complete list of compatible motorcycles, and the retrofit option remains under development.

Still, the prospect of adding significantly faster charging to existing electric motorcycles could be an important development for the brand.

There are several exciting announcements here, but I think the biggest takeaway is that Zero seems to be increasingly focused on making electric motorcycling more accessible through smaller and more affordable options.

For much of its 20-year history, Zero has been a pioneer in the electric motorcycle industry, often offering impressive performance and technology, but at prices that made its motorcycles difficult for many riders to justify. The bikes have long won acclaim, but $20k was a big ask.

The company’s more affordable X Line bikes have already demonstrated that Zero is interested in attracting riders who might never have considered one of its larger electric motorcycles. The street-legal XE takes that concept a step further, and Project Ventura could be an even more important addition.

I’m particularly intrigued by Zero’s explicit acknowledgment that millions of people have spent the last several years riding e-bikes and smaller electric motos, and that many of those riders may be ready to graduate to something bigger.

That’s an audience I’ve been watching grow for years. These are riders who are already comfortable with electric drivetrains, who appreciate the simplicity of twist-and-go riding, and who don’t necessarily have any attachment to gasoline engines or traditional motorcycle culture.

For those riders, a lightweight, fun electric motorcycle capable of 81 mph and priced below $8,000 could be an awfully compelling next step.

The new street-legal XE is similarly exciting, especially for riders who want to combine urban transportation with off-road adventures without needing a truck to haul their bike around.

During the late 60’s to the early 70’s the in thing in motorcycles was the street legal dirt bike. I had a 1971 model Kawasaki 125 street legal dirtbike that I bought for $525 and it was great for getting around as a kid. When this street legal type of EV bike goes below $5000 it could be the next big thing.

And while the new motorcycles are likely to get most of the attention, I wouldn’t overlook the DC fast-charging announcement. Charging speed has long been one of the biggest limitations facing electric motorcycles, particularly for riders interested in longer trips. A sub-30-minute charging stop isn’t quite gasoline-level convenience, but it’s getting much closer to something that can work for real motorcycle touring.

Of course, several important details remain unknown, and we’ll have to wait until 2027 to see how these products and technologies perform in the real world.

But taken together, these announcements suggest Zero is making a serious effort to expand beyond its traditional audience and build electric motorcycles for a much broader range of riders.

And after two decades of helping pioneer the electric motorcycle industry, that’s exactly the kind of evolution I’d like to see.

#4465. BMW's Tesla FSD Rival Hits City Streets In 2027

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

BMW's advanced driver assistance system (ADAS) is already pretty good and can smoothly cruise highways hands-free. However, BMW wants to up its ADAS game even further by expanding the system to include city driving in 2027. In other words, BMW's rival to Tesla Full Self-Driving (Supervised) is coming soon.

The navigation-guided, "partially automated" system will be able to use BMW maps to make turns, lane changes, navigate roundabouts, and even understand right-of-way situations, BMW announced on Monday. It can already handle some stop-and-go situations, and even stop for traffic lights, but this will be another step up.

"By extending partially automated driving functions to urban areas, we will offer our customers a real improvement in driving comfort—with confident driver assistance in true BMW style," said BMW board member Joachim Post in a statement. "The system will support them seamlessly along the navigation route, from motorways through country roads and into the city."

Much of the auto industry is racing to match Tesla's FSD with their own point-to-point driving systems for cities. Perhaps most importantly, BMW's perennial rival Mercedes-Benz is working on the technology with both Nvidia and Wayve. Rivian plans to launch an in-house point-to-point system to its cars next year.

BMW drivers will be able to see what the car is planning to do in BMW's Panoramic Vision dashboard. The screen in front of the driver will indicate the traffic it's seeing around itself, what it's currently doing, and all other relevant info. Since this is a Level 2 system, drivers will have to remain attentive.

Rollout for this new ADAS will start in Germany next year, with other markets following over time. (BMW didn't announce a timeline for a U.S. rollout.) The hardware for this new ADAS will be standard on several new models, like the BMW iX3, iX4, 3 Series, X5, and 7 Series. The software itself will be available via an over-the-air update, BMW says.

#4464. Automakers Want Congress to Permanently Ban Chinese Cars From the U.S.

The Alliance for Automotive Innovation, which represents dozens of car companies and other industry businesses, said vehicles made by Chinese brands carry ​surveillance risks.

Chinese vehicles have become a serious political issue in the United States in recent months, and earlier this week, the Alliance for Automotive Innovation—a lobbying group that represents a wide range of automakers from General Motors and Toyota to Ferrari and Porsche—weighed in on the hot-button issue. The president and CEO of the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, John Bozzella, said that Chinese vehicles should be permanently banned from the U.S. market, citing factors such as security concerns and unfair business practices.

“We need to protect the U.S. market from a flood of Chinese imports that carry surveillance risk and disadvantage current manufacturers that have made generational investments in ⁠American communities,” Bozzella said, according to Reuters.

Support for banning Chinese vehicles is a surprisingly bipartisan issue, as Senators Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) and Bernie Moreno (R-OH) co-authored the Connected Vehicle Security Act of 2026 earlier this year. The bill unanimously passed the Senate Commerce Committee this summer, and is expected to be voted on next week during the short “lame duck” legislative session ‌after the midterm elections. A version of the Connected Vehicle Security Act of 2026 in the House of Representatives has now amassed over 100 cosponsors, too.

But it isn’t just security concerns that have legacy automakers pushing for an outright ban on Chinese cars. Bozzella cited significant gains from those vehicles in the European market as further evidence that regulations are necessary, claiming that the European Union imported more than 1.1 million vehicles from China in the first eight months of 2026—more Chinese cars than the EU imported in all of 2025. The Volkswagen Group, one of the companies represented by the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, cited competition from Chinese automakers as part of its major restructuring earlier this year.

“Given the obvious national security risk and China’s pattern of unfair behavior, Congress should protect our defense and advanced manufacturing base and stop Chinese automakers from doing here what they’ve gotten away ‌with ⁠in Europe,” Bozzella said.

“I think it's an issue of economic security and national security," Slotkin told Road & Track in April. "You don't have to be a deep expert to understand that the Chinese Communist Party heavily subsidizes their industry, so they have a whole strategy of basically stealing our intellectual property—making stuff like cars and drones off of stuff that we've invented, and then heavily subsidizing them so that they undercut and kill the industry that they enter. They have a long history of doing that with drones, [and] the solar industry is ninety percent Chinese because of this very strategy."

Congressional aides and industry experts said there may not be enough time to approve the Chinese vehicle ban during this session if Democrats win control of Congress, according to Reuters. Even so, as momentum builds in both the House and Senate, legacy automakers remain hopeful. A 100-percent tariff on Chinese electric vehicles also remains in place.

A New York transplant hailing from the Pacific Northwest, Emmet White has a passion for anything that goes: cars, bicycles, planes, and motorcycles. After learning to ride at 17, Emmet worked in the motorcycle industry before joining Autoweek in 2022 and Road & Track in 2024. #4463. 2027 Harley-Davidson Sprint 440 Harkens Back to a Simpler Time

Harley-Davidson’s new entry-level motorcycle resurrects a classic name and its single-cylinder formula.

Given the price of, well, everything these days, affordability and accessibility are unsurprisingly hot buzzwords in the motorcycle industry. And brands that’ve embraced them are reaping the benefits. Bikes like Triumph’s 400 range and Royal Enfield’s 350 range—lightweight, inexpensive, modest-capacity single-cylinder—are practically flying off showroom floors. Up until now, that’s described nothing in Harley-Davidson’s stable, at least for US riders. But that changes with the 2027 Harley-Davidson Sprint 440.

While the Bar and Shield basically bleeds V-twins, the brand hasn’t only made two-cylinder bikes. Its earliest models, often called “Silent Gray Fellows,” had single-cylinder engines. And if the new Sprint 440’s name seems familiar to you, it’s because Harley sold single-powered bikes with that nameplate in the 1960s and 1970s.

While those Sprints were built in Italy, the US-market Sprint 440s will be built in Harley’s York, Pennsylvania factory. Admittedly, this new Sprint technically derives from the single-cylinder Harley that’s already been on sale elsewhere for several years: the X440 developed together with the Indian company Hero MotoCorp. But still, don’t cry heresy, Milwaukee faithful.

It might use a vintage name and manufacturing formula, but the 2027 Sprint 440 is a thoroughly modern Harley-Davidson. Its 440cc two-valve air/oil-cooled single-cylinder engine—fuel-injected, unlike the carbureted original Sprints—makes 27 hp and 28 pound-feet, sent to the rear wheel via a slip-assist clutch and six-speed transmission. That rear wheel is 17 inches in diameter, with the front being 19 inches; both are cast aluminum. And when the Sprint needs to stop, er, sprinting, you’ve got ABS-equipped disc brakes.

If that doesn’t seem like enough scream for this eagle, know that the Royal Enfield Meteor 350 cruiser’s 394cc single-cylinder engine makes 20 hp and 20 pound-feet. Also, according to the spec sheets, the Sprint 440 is slightly lighter: a claimed 412 pounds to the Meteor 350’s 421 pounds. The Sprint is that much lighter than the upcoming Triumph Bonneville T40 as well, though the Triumph’s 398cc liquid-cooled single makes 30 hp (and other Triumph 400 models make around 40 hp). But, in another accessibility nod, the Meteor 350’s and Bonneville T4’s seats are 30.1 and 32.2 inches high, respectively, while Harley claims a 26.4-inch laden seat height for the Sprint. All three of these bikes have preload-adjustable dual rear shocks, though unlike the other two, the Sprint 440’s forks are inverted.

See all results for used cars for sale near 83709

Moving on, the 2027 Harley-Davidson Sprint 440 has a color TFT display (something quickly becoming de rigeur). The 3.5-inch circular gauge shows a speedometer, tachometer, odometer, and trip meter as well as the usual warning lights and turn signals. Those turn signals, like the headlight and taillight, are LED. And there’s one of the other modern motorcycling necessities, a USB-C charging port, above the headlight. Additionally, Harley-Davidson will offer numerous accessories for the Sprint 440, including a windshield, engine guard, saddlebags, and (predictably) skull adornments. Also, if the regular seat isn’t the right height, there will be multiple seat options to dial in your proper fit.

OK, accessibility seems fine, but what about that affordability? When Harley-Davidson first announced it was resurrecting the Sprint, it claimed the bike would cost around $6000. As of this writing, U.S. pricing hasn’t been revealed. However, in Canada, the Sprint 440 will cost $8499 CAD, which is about $6100 at current exchange rates. That’s roughly $1000 more than a 2027 Royal Enfield Meteor 350, though it’s around what Triumph charges for its 400 models.

But, crucially, it’s almost $4000 less expensive than Harley’s current entry-level model, the 975cc Nightster. And while everything’s expensive these days, four grand still buys quite a bit of gasoline for riding. We’ll just have to wait until spring 2027 to see if the Sprint 440 hits the ground running.

#4462. BYD’s 3,000-hp EV crashes at about 280 mph — Watch the driver escape unharmed

BYD’s electric supercar delivers an insane nearly 3,000 hp from four electric motors. During a high-speed test, the Yangwang U9 Extreme crashed at about 280 mph, but the driver walked away unharmed.

The Yangwang U9 Xtreme is a “dream car,” as BYD calls it, a souped-up, track-focused version of its electric hypercar.

After it became the world’s fastest production car last year, reaching a top speed of 496.22 km/h, or about 308 mph, BYD is attempting to beat it by breaking the 500 km/h (310 mph) mark.

The Yangwang U9 Xtreme features the world’s first mass-produced 1,200V ultra-high-voltage platform and BYD’s e4 platform.

The quad-motor setup is the first in the world rated at 30,000 rpm, BYD said, delivering nearly 3,000 hp (3,000 PS) combined.

While BYD is preparing to attempt a run this month, the company shared a video of the Yangwang U9 Xtreme crashing in a violent high-speed test.

During the first run, it clocked over 350 km/h (217 mph), no problem. On the second run, it hit over 420 km/h (261 mph).

However, during the third run, BYD was attempting to reach over 450 km/h (280 mph) when the vehicle violently crashed into the guardrail and continued spinning out of control. You can see some of the footage from inside the vehicle.

BYD said that after a comprehensive medical exam, the hospital found the driver in good health with no serious injuries.

When I was still in law enforcement, we did some pursuit driving training and you learn a lot about the dynamics of a vehicle. It's amazing just how quickly and badly something can go wrong at just 100 mph let alone nearly triple that speed. The fact is that the average person can't drive to the max limits of a basic car like a Corolla let alone super cars.

Is it time to reign in the HP and speed wars? Do we need vehicles that can do 0-60 in less than 3 seconds? Unless these companies begin to require 40+ hour specialized training courses in order to buy/operate these high HP vehicles today, then maybe it's time to stop the silly push for more.

And BTW. No matter what the performance levels are of any cars today, I still feel that it would be smart to push legal driving age to at least 17 or 18 instead of 16 and make getting a DL harder to do with way more emphasis on driver's education training.

The vehicle’s high-strength carbon-fiber cabin also held up impressively despite the front and rear damage.

It didn’t take long for BYD to try again, reaching a top speed of 457.89 km/h (284.5 mph) on the next run. Jiang Gong, one of Yangwang’s riders, said he sees some leeway and believes it can break 500 km/h (310 mph).

At the end of the video, BYD said (translated into English), “The ultimate pursuit has no end; the summit will eventually be reached.”

#4461. Ford's Privacy Promise Includes A 'Quasi-80s Mode' To Dumb-Down Connected Cars

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Modern cars are enormously talented at producing gobs of information about drivers. How hard they smash the brakes, where they frequently navigate to, or even what in-car features they use the most. It makes it incredible difficult to draw a line between what portion of an automaker is a car company or a tech company.

Ford would like you to know that it won't be that difficult to tell your car to zip its mouth about driver data—if it's wearing a Blue Oval on the grille, that is.

Ford also shares what it does with that data and (most importantly) how you, the driver, can turn data sharing off.

A car cannot simultaneously refuse to tell Ford where it is and also ask Ford to give it information relevant to the world around it (like live traffic data). That means if you choose to turn off connected navigation, internet connectivity, and location features in the Ford app, you'll lose some functionality within the car. And doing that would certainly make the car have a more '80s experience, after all.

The trade-off for Ford is that it uses that data to help tailor its vehicles to include features that owners want. No data means that Ford will need to find another way to customize in-car features to fit a less-connected digital experience.

Ford CEO Jim Farley also recently mentioned that the company will lean on digital subscriptions to help boost revenue with vehicles like the uber-cheap Ford Fathom. The caveat there is "digital," which means that vehicles that ditch connectivity could also be a lost cause on digital subscription revenue. And that's the ultimate compromise that owners will need to decide.

The good news is, Ford is at least being transparent about owner choice. That's the entire point according to Jones: "The trust really comes from transparency. It’s our job to be as radically transparent as we can be."

#4460. Tesla cuts FSD’s speed margin from 50% to 10% over the limit in Europe

Tesla’s driver-assistance system in Europe can no longer be set to drive 50% over the speed limit. The Netherlands’ RDW, which approved the system in April, confirmed today that it signed off on an update capping the speed margin at 10% and officially renaming “FSD Supervised” to Tesla Assisted Driving.

The changes land weeks before EU member states could vote on approving the system across the bloc, and they match the conditions Germany set last month.

The RDW’s notice is the clearest official confirmation of how the system was configured when the Dutch regulator approved FSD Supervised on April 10. The “speed margin,” which lets the system deviate from the detected limit for “safety and traffic flow,” could go up to +50%. On a 100 km/h highway, that’s 150 km/h. In a 30 km/h city zone, it’s 45 km/h.

Now the margin tops out at +10%. It also resets to 0% every time the car starts, and the RDW says other speed-related functions are now disabled by default. It didn’t say which ones.

The new name shows up on the in-car display, in the owner’s manual, and in other driver information on HW4 vehicles. Tesla pushes all of it over the air.

The RDW describes the update as “several minor changes” that Tesla asked it to assess. The regulator says it checked the implementation, found no adverse or unintended effects, and folded the changes into the existing type approval without amending or extending it. It also stresses that the rename doesn’t change what the system does. It’s still driver assistance, and the driver is still responsible.

The RDW notified the nine member states that recognize its approval: Belgium, Croatia, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, and Slovenia. That’s 10 countries counting the Netherlands, up from eight at the start of October.

The EU-wide decision still sits with the Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles (TCMV). The RDW says those talks are confidential and won’t comment on them. As we reported, the EU pushed the vote to December at the earliest, and passing it takes a qualified majority: 15 of 27 member states representing at least 65% of the EU population.

Speed has been the biggest problem for Tesla’s file in Brussels. In June, Sweden asked the EU to reject FSD unless Tesla removed the ability to set speeds above the posted limit. In September, a Brussels pedestrian safety group found the system speeding in 55% of the 30 km/h segments it tested, in a country that had already approved it. France has cited urban speeding as one of its reasons for refusing to recognize the Dutch approval.

Then, on October 6, Germany’s Transport Ministry said it would back EU approval after Tesla agreed to drop the “Full Self-Driving” name, which the ministry called misleading, and to cap speed tolerance at 10%. Today’s RDW update delivers both.

But 10% isn’t what Sweden asked for. Sweden wanted no setting above the limit at all. Several European countries are known for enforcing speed limits strictly.

Good, but that’s only part of the problem. Tesla’s biggest issue with FSD right now is that it doesn’t properly detect the speed limits.

Doing 10% over the limit in North America is almost expected. However, in Europe you can get a speeding ticket for 5 kms over the limit by an automated camera/radar system. When I rent a car over there I drive the posted limit.

Being locked at 10% over the limit doesn’t mean much if you don’t know the actual limit.

The name change is needed globally and it is past due. “Tesla Assisted Driving” describes what the system does. Meanwhile, Tesla still sells the exact same kind of software in the US as “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” for $99 a month. If it’s misleading in Berlin, it’s misleading in California.

Practically, this update gets Tesla Germany’s vote. The question for December is whether a 10% cap is enough for France, Italy, and Spain, or whether Sweden’s zero-tolerance line wins out.

#4459. The Ford Bronco Frostwarden Makes 1200 HP, Thanks to Its Megazilla 2.0 Supercharged V-8

This search-and-rescue machine, revealed at SEMA, is what happens when Ford throws everything it has at a Bronco.

The folks at Ford brought one of the wildest Broncos we’ve ever seen to the 2026 SEMA Show this year. It’s called “Frostwarden” ... and it has 1200 horsepower.

How’d Ford extract that much horsepower from a Bronco? Well, it sure doesn’t use any version of the production engines. Instead, Ford put the also-new Megazilla 2.0 crate motor under the hood. This 7.3-liter V-8 is paired here with a 3.0-liter Gen 6 Whipple supercharger; it also has a stronger block, supercharger-specific camshaft, upgraded pistons, larger fuel injectors, and a different belt drive and damper. As a package, Ford is claiming 1200 hp and 1000 pound-feet of torque when run with race fuel. (No, it didn’t quote a pump gas number.)

The idea behind the rest of the rig was to put together a package that could be used as an arctic search-and-rescue machine. To that end, it has a custom Bilstein suspension, 74Weld portal gear lifts, upgraded Dana driveline, and 18-inch Weld bead-lock wheels wrapped in 42-inch BFGoodrich tires. It’s absolutely enormous, and gives off the impression that one could drive it anywhere, which is largely the point.

This Bronco is festooned with accessories front to back. Rigid lights should help show the way through snowstorms. A spare wheels/tire and pair of toolboxes sit atop the roof. There’s a shovel, recovery rope, fuel jugs, and more. Plus, Ford outfitted the interior with color-matching seats and accents. There’s even a “Megazilla” emblem in the steering wheel rim to make sure you don’t forget this beast has 1200 horsepower ready to unleash.

Unfortunately, Ford explicitly says these vehicle “is not available for purchase,” and we suspect something like it never will be from your local Ford dealer. However, it serves as proof that you can shoehorn a 7.3-liter supercharged V-8 under the (admittedly bulged) hood of a Bronco, and what’s not to love about that?

#4457. Gas Vs. Electric: Which BMW Goes Further Without Stopping For Fuel?

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Range anxiety won't stop being an issue among EV buyers for a while. Customers are still new to EVs, and the entire idea of charging a car is still foreign to many people. So EV range will always be compared to gas-powered range, because that's what most drivers are used to. However, EVs are getting close and closer, if not sometimes surpassing, the range of internal combustion cars, so it's worth showing how the two different technologies actually handle the same distances. In this new video from Chasing Cars, you get to see just that: A BMW iX3 takes on a piston-powered BMW X3 in a range test.

The test was pretty simple, as the two hosts drove a BMW iX3 50 xDrive and a BMW X3 M50 xDrive from Sydney, Australia to Byron Bay. They used normal routes, kept both cars in their Eco settings, and kept the climate controls on their most efficient settings. Both cars were kept at speed limits, and both drivers stopped off if they needed to for whatever reason. So it was indicative of what a real-life road trip would be like.

From start to finish, the trip was 459.8 miles (740 km). When they started, the electric iX3 showed an estimated range of 692 km (430 miiles), so not enough to make it. But even after about 30 km into the trip, the gas-powered X3 M50 showed an estimated 784 km (487 miles) of range, which is quite a bit more than the iX3. Oddly, though, judging by the iX3's efficiency early one, the math indicated that it would make the trip with a few kWh to spare.

It's interesting to see the gas-powered car have so much more range, not because it's gas but because it's the big engine version of the X3. The M50 packs a 3.0-liter turbocharged I6, and while it's a mild hybrid, it makes 393 horsepower and 428 lb-ft of torque. It's the thirstiest of all X3s, at least until the X3 M comes out. But that doesn't make it the most powerful SUV BMW makes in this segment. The iX3 M50 is more powerful, with 463 horsepower and 476 lb-ft of torque.

Ultimately, the iX3 was able to do 747 km (464 miles) on one charge, which is significantly more than the EPA-rated 434 miles of range. It fell just 23 km (14.2 miles) short of Byron Bay. The X3 M50? It not only made it to the destination, it had 332 km (206 miles) of range left in the tank. So that clearly means it wins the test. However, the iX3 was still massively impressive, and has the sort of range few other EVs on the planet can match. So even though BMW's mild-hybrid straight-six is ultra efficient and tough to beat, that doesn't diminish the iX3's achievement.
